extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, biotech IP scholars, law professors, law students, and USPTO examiners interested in written description and enablement issues in biotech patents
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of the Federal Circuit's written description jurisprudence (the 'Lilly' doctrine) as applied to biotechnology patent claims, with comparison to the enablement requirement and discussion of related doctrines (patent eligibility, obviousness, PTO practice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description should police introduction of new matter only
rubrics_metrics.description: The written description requirement should be used only to police against the introduction of new matter into claims, and not as a separate requirement of patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author's normative position: written description ought to guard against adding new subject matter post-filing rather than functioning as an independent substantive patentability hurdle. The post criticizes the expansion of 'Lilly' written description into a separate basis for invalidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lilly written description doctrine (Regents of UC v. Eli Lilly)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Lilly written description requirement (from Regents of UC v. Eli Lilly, 1997) has been relied on by the Federal Circuit to invalidate originally filed claims (e.g., claims directed to the insulin gene) and has been expanded in reach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The blog traces the doctrine's origin and notes its expansion in both the courts and the PTO. Treat as a distinct doctrine the court has used to police claim scope and sufficiency of disclosure, beyond classical enablement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific structural disclosure required for broad functional claims (University of Rochester)
rubrics_metrics.description: In University of Rochester v. G.D. Searle the Federal Circuit found claims invalid because 'the specification did not specifically describe any non-steroidal compound that would perform the claimed function.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a claim recites a broad function (e.g., 'a method for selectively inhibiting PGHS-2 ... comprising administering a non-steroidal compound'), the specification may be required to identify specific compounds or structural examples that perform that function; absent such specifics, written description may be found lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to 'describe some way of performing the claimed methods' (Ariad)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Circuit in Ariad stated that '[R]egardless of whether the asserted claims recite a compound, Ariad still must describe some way of performing the claimed methods.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional method claims that broadly claim any method achieving a result require the specification to describe at least some manner of performing the claimed method; mere recitation of the result without disclosure of a way to achieve it can fail written description.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Descriptive link' requirement between disclosed structures and claimed function
rubrics_metrics.description: The Ariad majority concluded there was 'no descriptive link between the table of decoy molecules and reducing NF-kB activity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court used lack of an explicit link between structural examples and the claimed functional outcome as a basis for invalidity. The blog criticizes this as a novel/conclusory requirement created by the majority (i.e., the court coined a 'descriptive link' requirement rather than relying on established doctrine).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commensurateness / breadth constraint: disclosure must bear the weight of claim scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims can be invalidated when 'the disclosure is insufficient to bear the weight of the vast scope of these generic claims.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A key evaluative standard is whether the specification's disclosure is commensurate with the breadth of the claims; overly broad claims that claim more than the specification justifies are susceptible to invalidation under the written description doctrine (as applied by Lilly cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement (Section 112): enable full scope without undue experimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: To survive the enablement requirement the specification 'must describe the manner and process of making and using the invention so as to enable a person of skill in the art to making use the full scope of the invention without undue experimentation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Linn (concurrence) and the blog emphasize that enablement is the traditional, established doctrine for policing claim scope — i.e., disclosure must enable the full scope of claimed subject matter. The post argues enablement, not written description, is the appropriate tool for policing overbroad functional claims, though courts have struggled to articulate a workable standard for policing claim scope via enablement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophetic examples may satisfy written description in chemical arts
rubrics_metrics.description: The court acknowledged that 'prophetic examples are routinely used to satisfy the written description requirement in the chemical arts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although prophetic (i.e., hypothetical/future-directed) examples can often satisfy written description for chemical or biotech inventions, the court in Ariad still found the particular prophetic disclosure insufficient — illustrating that the adequacy of prophetic examples is fact-specific and may be judged against the claimed scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent eligibility constraint: cannot claim a natural phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that 'wholly encompassing a natural phenomenon' may be patent ineligible; Lilly argued Ariad's claims were patent ineligible for wholly encompassing a natural phenomenon, but the Federal Circuit avoided that issue by deciding written description instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent eligibility (e.g., exclusion of natural phenomena) remains a separate ground to evaluate claims; courts may choose to decide a case on written description or enablement grounds without reaching eligibility, but eligibility is a distinct doctrinal filter for claim validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness can render written description issues moot
rubrics_metrics.description: In In re Kubin the panel declined to address written description as moot because the claims were invalid based on obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obviousness (patentability under 35 U.S.C. §103) can serve as an alternative and dispositive ground for invalidity; if claims are obvious in view of the prior art, courts may not address written description issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO practice: aggressive application of Lilly written description separate from enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Office has become much more aggressive in applying Lilly written description as a requirement of patentability separate and distinct from the enablement requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner practice and PTO policy increasingly invoke Lilly-style written description scrutiny; practitioners should be aware that the PTO may apply written description as an independent hurdle beyond enablement when examining biotech claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain-specific expansion: Lilly applied originally to biomolecules and then to method claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Lilly written description had previously been applied primarily to biomolecule claims (nucleic acids and antibodies); University of Rochester marked the first instance applying the doctrine to method claims, and Ariad continued that trend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The scope of the written description doctrine has expanded from structural biomolecule claims to functional and method claims in the biotech context, meaning practitioners drafting biotech claims must consider both structural disclosure and method/function linkages.
